commentary: Aquinas opens by explaining why Aristotle refuses to settle anything before first laying out every difficulty the coming science must face. He gives four reasons drawn from Aristotle's own text. First, resolving a question later is nothing but untying a knot one has already examined, and no one can loosen a knot without first looking closely at how it is tied. Second, a mind caught in doubt is bound much as a body is bound by chains; just as a man with his feet tied cannot walk forward, a mind that has not faced its perplexities cannot advance toward the truth. Third, someone who has not marked out the difficulty beforehand is like a traveler with no fixed destination, unable to know whether he has arrived. Fourth, a good judge must hear the arguments on both sides of a dispute before deciding, and the reader of this science must do the same. Aquinas stresses that this is Aristotle's habitual practice throughout his works, but here it takes a distinctive form: rather than raising each doubt individually as a topic comes up, he gathers, in one sweep, every perplexity bearing on the whole science of first causes and universal being before beginning to answer any of them. What follows, then, is not confusion but a deliberate map of the terrain - the full set of questions concerning causes, principles, substance, unity, genera, and the perishable and imperishable - that the rest of the work will address one by one in proper order.

Aquinas walks through several linked puzzles here. On whether one science can study all the causes at once, he notes the objection that immobile realities have no moving or final cause in the ordinary sense, since these involve change; yet he shows Aristotle's eventual answer is that wisdom studies form, end, and, where applicable, moving cause together, because these are not opposed to one another the way rival principles would be. On whether the common axioms, such as the impossibility of simultaneously affirming and denying the same thing, fall under this same science, Aquinas explains that they belong to it precisely because it studies being as such, and every axiom concerns being universally; other sciences merely borrow these axioms as already known, while the philosopher alone defends them against those who deny them, arguing dialectically rather than demonstrating them from anything prior. On whether one science treats all substances and their attributes together, Aquinas holds that metaphysics considers substance under its common character, and therefore also considers the attributes common to all being, even though it defines substance rather than demonstrating it, while it does demonstrate substance's proper attributes. Finally, on whether separate Forms and mathematical intermediates exist besides sensible things, Aquinas traces the Platonists' reasoning - a double abstraction, first of universal from particular, then of mathematical objects from sensible matter - and lays out Aristotle's objections: an eternal duplicate of a perishable man is absurd, and positing separate mathematical heavens or a separate medicine multiplies unwanted intermediates without warrant.

Here Aquinas takes up two connected doubts about principles. The first asks whether genera - such as the broad category to which a thing belongs - are the true principles of things, or whether the ultimate parts composing a thing hold that role instead, as letters compose a syllable rather than the general notion of 'articulate sound' doing so. Aquinas resolves this by a distinction: genera do serve as principles of knowing, because a definition is built from genus and specific difference, and to define something is to know what it is. But being a principle of our knowledge is not the same as being a principle of a thing's actual being. What genuinely constitutes a thing in reality is closer to its concrete parts or its form and matter, not the abstract universal under which we classify it. The second doubt asks, granting that genera are somehow principles, whether the highest and most universal genera - being, unity, and the like - are more truly principles than the narrower genera predicated immediately of individuals. Aquinas notes that this question only has force for those, like the Platonists, who take universals to be separately subsisting things; on that assumption, the most universal reality would indeed be most fundamental. But once one denies that universals exist apart from the things they are said of, the specific and proximate forms - nearer to the individual - turn out to be the more genuine principles, since form generally causes and constitutes a thing more directly than remote, generic matter does.

This chapter gathers Aquinas's treatment of four of the hardest aporiai. First, whether something exists beyond matter as a cause in its own right - some separate form. Aquinas notes the case for it: without an ungenerated principle, generation would either regress endlessly or never get started at all. Yet it is unclear where to stop positing such separate forms, since obviously no separate 'house' exists apart from particular houses; Aquinas signals that the eventual answer distinguishes immaterial substances, which really are separate, from the forms of material things, which never exist apart from matter even though the intellect can grasp them universally. Second, whether the principles of things are numerically one or only alike in kind; Aquinas points ahead to Book Twelve, where intrinsic principles like matter and form turn out to be the same across individuals only by analogy, while separate substances are each numerically singular. Third, whether perishable and imperishable things share the same principles. Aquinas carefully unpacks Aristotle's critique of the mythical theologians who made the gods immortal through eating nectar and ambrosia, and of Empedocles, whose strife and love cannot consistently explain why some things last forever and others do not. Fourth, whether being and unity are themselves the substance of things, as Plato and the Pythagoreans held, or instead qualities of some other underlying subject; Aquinas shows how both Parmenides's collapse of all things into one and Zeno's argument against indivisible unity create genuine difficulty, pointing forward to Aristotle's later teaching that a thing is one simply through its own essence, without needing a separately existing 'unity itself.'

Aquinas here follows Aristotle's puzzle over whether numbers, solid bodies, surfaces, lines, and points are themselves substances. The case for treating them as such runs through elimination: qualities, relations, and quantities are all said of some underlying subject and are not themselves a 'this,' so if body, too, fails to qualify, nothing would remain to count as substance at all. Yet a further problem arises, because surface, line, and point seem in some ways more substantial than body itself, since body is bounded and defined by them while they do not depend on body for their own definition - a solid is understood through its surfaces, a surface through its lines, a line through its points. Against this, Aquinas explains Aristotle's counter-argument: a given shape, such as half of a cube, is only potentially, not actually, present within an undivided solid, much as a statue is only potentially present in an unworked block of stone; so surfaces, lines, and points exist in bodies merely potentially rather than as actual substantial parts. A further difficulty concerns generation: when bodies are joined or divided, their boundaries seem to come into being and pass away, yet without any of the ordinary marks of generation or corruption, since there is no matter out of which a point or surface could be made or into which it could dissolve - much like the 'now' of time, which is never generated yet is never quite the same moment twice. Aquinas notes that Aristotle's eventual solution treats these mathematical entities not as substances but as accidents of quantity belonging to composite bodies.

Aquinas closes the book's survey of doubts with three further questions. First, why posit separate Forms at all, once sensible things and mathematical intermediates are already granted? He reconstructs the Platonist reasoning: just as many individual sensible men share one specific nature without being numerically one, so too many equal triangles or lines share one mathematical species without being numerically identical; if that is all there is, then the principles of things would be determinate only in kind and never in number, which the Platonists found intolerable, and so they added the Forms to secure something genuinely one in number beneath the many. Aquinas notes Aristotle's eventual reply that moving causes are indeed numerically determinate, while formal principles shared by a species are rightly determinate only in kind, so no separate Form is actually needed. Second, whether the elements or principles of things exist potentially or in some other, actual way; Aquinas shows the difficulty runs both directions, since positing them as already actual seems to require something still prior, while treating them as merely potential seems to make nothing actually exist at all, and he points ahead to the resolution that act is simply prior to potency, so that a first principle must exist actually. Third, whether principles are universal or individual; universals, predicated commonly, seem unable to be a 'this' and so unable to be substances, yet only the universal is properly an object of scientific knowledge, leaving the puzzle Aristotle later untangles by distinguishing subsisting singulars from the universal manner in which the intellect knows them.
